entry.title: SIX UNEARNED RUNS SQUANDERED, NINE UNANSWERED RETURNED — DETROIT'S FIVE-RUN EIGHTH TURNS THE EVENING ON ITS HEAD, AND THE CENTRAL'S DEADLOCK BREAKS AGAINST CHICAGO: TIGERS 11, WHITE SOX 8
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 73 · Saturday, the Nineteenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SIX UNEARNED RUNS SQUANDERED, NINE UNANSWERED RETURNED — DETROIT'S FIVE-RUN EIGHTH TURNS THE EVENING ON ITS HEAD, AND THE CENTRAL'S DEADLOCK BREAKS AGAINST CHICAGO: TIGERS 11, WHITE SOX 8

Hao-Yu Lee, whose fumble at third opened Chicago's six-run first, atones with four hits and the tying homer; McGonigle drives in four, three of them on the triple that sent Peters into a fence-pole; and with Cleveland winning by the lake, the White Sox wake a full game out of first with their wild-card cushion pared to one

The Tigers of Detroit will watch October from their parlors this autumn, which is precisely what makes them dangerous company in September: a club with nothing left to defend and every appetite for mischief. Chicago was taught the lesson by installments. The visitors nicked a run on a wild pitch in the first; the White Sox answered with six in the home half without earning a single one of them — a run home on a wild pitch of Sears' own, the door swung wide by Hao-Yu Lee's fumble at third, Colson Montgomery's three-run double and Vargas's knock among the traffic through nine batters. When Miguel Vargas added his two-and-thirtieth homer in the third, the count stood 8-2 and the evening had every look of a formality.

It was instead a slow confiscation. Kevin McGonigle singled home a run in the third, then emptied the bases in the fifth with a three-run triple to right-center — the drive on which the right fielder Peters, lunging and missing, met a fence-pole at a full run, as the ward below records — and Lee, of all men, set about repaying his error with interest: a run-scoring double in the sixth, then a two-run homer off Newcomb in the eighth that squared the account at eight apiece. Dingler's single put Detroit ahead, and Riley Greene's one-and-twentieth, two runs the richer, closed a five-run frame — nine unanswered runs in all. Sommers threw two perfect innings with five strikeouts for the victory; Jansen sealed his one-and-twentieth save. Lee's final ledger: four hits, a double, the tying homer, three driven in, and one error atoned in full.

Now the morning's arithmetic, which stings the South Side twice over. Cleveland won by the lake — the milestone desk sings the how of it — and so Friday morning's deadlock is Saturday's one-game Cleveland lead, nine-and-seventy wins to Chicago's eight-and-seventy. The tiebreaker remains Chicago's, the season series banked seven games to six, so the Cleveland men must still finish clear rather than level; but the White Sox' own cushion for the American's last wild-card chair is likewise down to a single game over Texas, and these same Tigers return to the South Side this very afternoon at ten past two. "Yeah, it's tough. No way about it," said the manager Venable. "Obviously you have a special first inning there and get the lead. Just weren't able to get any outs." Peters, nursing his bruises, spoke the professional's creed: "The only thing we can control is what we do tomorrow."

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE CAPTAIN OF THE YANKEES GOES BACK TO THE SHELF — JUDGE'S CALF STRAIN IS NAMED, WITH OCTOBER UNPROMISED; PETERS MEETS A FENCE-POLE; AND SAN FRANCISCO'S WEBB IS DONE FOR THE SEASON BY A BLISTER

The gravest cot belongs to the captain. The stiffness that lifted Aaron Judge from Wednesday's game in Minneapolis — entered in this paper's ward on Thursday — has a name now: a strain of the right calf, found by Thursday's examination in Phoenix, and it sends him to the ten-day invalid list this very day. The club will neither grade the strain's severity nor guess at a date, and the wires note that even the mildest of the kind commonly asks two or three weeks — with barely more than one remaining before October. Asked plainly whether his captain would return for the playoffs, the manager Boone answered: "I don't know. I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires." What is certain is the cost in the near term: Judge misses the Phoenix weekend and the four-game engagement with Tampa Bay that opens Tuesday at his own Stadium, with the East itself in the balance. The utility man Schuemann travels to meet the club. "There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge," said Boone, "but we have high expectations. Those don't change now." His men made the words good for one night at least, as the card below relates.

The lesser cots: Chicago's Tristan Peters chased McGonigle's fifth-inning drive to right-center, missed it by a lunge, and struck a pole supporting the outfield fence at a full run; he lay on the grass a minute or two before leaving with the trainer, and the verdict — a contusion of the left shoulder and ribs, day to day — reads far kinder than the collision looked. And San Francisco has shelved Logan Webb, gone to the fifteen-day list with a blistered right middle finger, the stint dated back to Tuesday — arithmetic that quietly ends his regular season.

THE MILESTONE DESK: THE THOUSANDTH RUN DRIVEN HOME ARRIVES BY THUNDERCLAP — RAMÍREZ JOINS EARL AVERILL IN CLEVELAND'S OWN BOOK, AND OLSON'S FORTIETH CROWNS A CLINCHING NIGHT

In the sixth inning by the lake, with the Central's lead in the balance, José Ramírez struck a solo home run — the two hundred seven-and-ninetieth of his life, measured a foot past four hundred — and the run it drove home was the thousandth of his career. The house rose to him when the figure flashed upon the videoboard as he took his station at third in the seventh. Only Earl Averill, at one thousand four-and-eighty, has driven home more in all the franchise's annals, and among active players Ramírez — four-and-thirty years old as of Thursday — becomes just the twelfth man to the figure, joining a roll that includes Freeman, Goldschmidt, Arenado, Machado, and Trout. "I like to use those round numbers," said the manager Vogt. "Ten years of 100 RBIs. When you break it down that way, it's incredible what he has accomplished, and he's not even close to being done, right?" The second baseman Bazzana testified to the dugout's view: "We all looked at each other, and everyone's got a smile on their face. He's an incredible, incredible player." The milestone was no ornament, either — Ramírez also singled home the tying run an inning before his thunder, and the victory put Cleveland atop the Central alone, as the lead columns sing.

And at Houston, on the very night Atlanta punched its October ticket, Matt Olson struck a two-run blow in the ninth for his fortieth home run of the year — his second season of forty as a Brave, a company that holds only Hank Aaron with eight, Eddie Mathews with four, and Acuña and Andruw Jones with two apiece. Since 2018, the wires observe, only Schwarber, Judge, and Ohtani have struck more home runs than Olson's three hundred three. His center fielder Harris rendered the scouting report in full: "Yeah, he's pretty good."

THE OCTOBER DESK: ATLANTA PUNCHES AN EIGHTH TICKET IN NINE YEARS, THREE CLUBS SHARE THE NATIONAL'S WILD-CARD ROW TO THE DECIMAL, AND THE WEEKEND STANDS THICK WITH CLINCHINGS-IN-WAITING

The Braves are formally through the gate: Friday's victory at Houston, sung in the card below, clinched Atlanta a postseason berth for the eighth time in nine years. The clinching arm belonged to Tyler Mahle, whose earned-run figure since arriving from San Francisco at the deadline stands at 1.28 — third among all qualified starters since the fourth of August, behind only the Yankee Schlittler and Philadelphia's Luzardo. "It's just exciting to be part of such a good team," said the veteran, bound now for the first playoff start of his life. The East is not yet sewn on: Atlanta leads Philadelphia by five with eight to play, and to clinch the division before leaving Houston on Sunday night the Braves must sweep while the Phillies drop one of two at Flushing.

Beneath them, the National's wild-card row has closed to a dead heat of rare perfection: the Cubs and Phillies both lost, the Padres won an eleventh game in twelve, and all three now stand at five-and-eighty wins against nine-and-sixty defeats — three clubs, three chairs, the order a matter of tiebreakers alone, with San Diego seated third having lost both season series. Arizona, five back after a third straight defeat, is the only pursuer left with a case. And the clinchings queue up behind: Boston can seal its berth as early as this very day at Tampa Bay, other scoreboards consenting; San Diego can seal its own as soon as tomorrow; and crowned Milwaukee's magic number for the National's first-round bye — any combination of Brewer victories and Atlanta defeats — stands at three, with the club one win shy of its own franchise record of seven-and-ninety, set only last season, and two clear of the field for the game's best ledger.

THE CONVALESCENT DESK: GOOD BULLETINS FROM THE CHAMPIONS' WARD — SNELL WILL TAKE THE BALL AGAIN, OHTANI SWINGS AT COACH'S PITCHING, AND DÍAZ RETURNS TO FIGHT FOR A NINTH INNING OF HIS OWN

The Dodgers' invalid list, which has shadowed these columns all week, sent up three encouraging dispatches in a single day. Blake Snell, whose groin ended Wednesday's start after an inning, threw from ninety feet before Friday's game and came away well — no imaging was even ordered. "Happy that we caught it early," said the manager Roberts, who expects the left-hander to make one more regular-season start without limitation; since the eleventh of August his earned-run figure stands at 1.01 across seven turns. Shohei Ohtani took the next step of his own convalescence, hitting coach-pitched batting practice and emerging sound; he builds up strictly as a batsman — the mound is finished for his year — and the earliest the list releases him is Wednesday. Having stayed behind to mend while the flag was clinched at Cincinnati, the great man missed Thursday's champagne altogether; he will have to wait upon a deeper October toast.

And Edwin Díaz is back in uniform, activated from his second shelving of the season with the neck inflammation healed — the corresponding move sending down Landon Knack, the same man who banked four innings in Thursday's clincher, as this paper sang only yesterday; baseball's ledgers keep a cold sort of books. Díaz threw a scoreless ninth in the rout the card records, the fastball averaging 97.6 miles to the hour, a full tick above his season's figure. "The fastball had that life," said Roberts. "And then the slider — once you have that fastball, the slider is pretty lethal." The three-time All-Star, signed last winter to close, now auditions like any September hopeful for a place in the October bullpen. The champions rebuild themselves piece by piece, and the calendar just barely obliges.

THE BUSH-LEAGUE DESK: A SAVE, A STRIKEOUT, AND A PERFECT BACKFLIP — AMARILLO PUNCTUATES ITS PENNANT-CLINCHER IN THE GRAND MANNER

The desk closes among the bushes, where the Double-A Amarillo Sod Poodles — Arizona's outpost in the Texas League — punched their ticket to the league Finals with an 8-7 decision over Frisco on Friday night, one evening after erasing a six-run deficit with their season at the wall. The finishing flourish belonged to the right-hander Alfred Morillo, who recorded the game-ending strikeout to seal the save, ripped off his glove, and executed a perfect backflip in one unbroken motion; his catcher Barriga sprinted to the mound and the whole roster spilled out behind him. The wires reckon the left-hander Jefry Yan the reigning artist of the strikeout celebration, but concede this was something else entirely. Amarillo — whose ranks include Druw Jones, son of the same Andruw enshrined in the milestone desk's forty-homer company above — opens a best-of-three for the title against a Springfield club stocked with Cardinal prospects on Sunday, chasing a third Texas League crown in seven years. If a semifinal merits the backflip, the Herald trembles to imagine the choreography a pennant would loose.

The Rest of the Card

THE OPENER'S GAMBIT MISFIRES AND THE LONG MAN MENDS ALL — CANTILLO'S SIX SPOTLESS INNINGS CARRY THE FOREST CITY NINE TO THE SUMMIT ALONE: FOREST CITY NINE 5, ATHLETICS 3

Gelof greeted the opener Espino with a three-run homer before an out was recorded, and Cleveland spent the rest of the evening un-digging: Joey Cantillo gave six innings of two hits behind him for his tenth victory, Rocchio doubled two home in the fourth, José Ramírez singled the game level and then struck the milestone thunder the desk above enshrines, and Bazzana's fifteenth supplied the lead for good. Smith sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save. Three straight now for the Forest City nine, alone atop the Central by one — though the tiebreaker still wears a Chicago uniform, as the lead columns weigh.

THE THIRD PITCH OF THE EVENING TRAVELS FOUR HUNDRED EIGHT-AND-THIRTY FEET — ANTHONY DRIVES IN THREE, AND THE RAYS' STREAK DIES AT SIX: FENWAY MEN 4, RAYS 2

Roman Anthony tore into the third pitch of the night for a leadoff homer the machines measured at four hundred eight-and-thirty feet, then delivered his first career hit with the bases full — a two-run single an inning later — and Boston never trailed. Suarez carried one run into the sixth, and Miller, working around a bases-loaded ninth in which Simpson grounded out to end it, banked his fifth save. Tampa Bay went without a hit with runners in scoring position all night; the streak of six is dead, and the East's lead over New York is pared to four with the four-game reckoning at the Stadium opening Tuesday. The Fenway men, their bruised catcher still resting, may seal their October berth this very day, other scoreboards consenting.

SIX WALKS UNDO THE STRIKEOUT KING AND A NEW MAN THROWS FOUR SPOTLESS — THE RANGERS DRAW DEAD LEVEL ATOP THE WEST: RANGERS 7, MAPLE LEAF NINE 1

The heavyweight bill this desk commended on Friday came apart inside three innings: Dylan Cease, the American's strikeout sovereign, walked six men in two and two-thirds and was charged four runs — one of them earned, Toronto's three errors underwriting the rest — while Texas drew ten walks in all. Rocker labored through four and a third before Justin Williams threw four spotless innings for the victory; Burger doubled, drove in two, and the West is a dead heat at last, Houston and Texas level at seven-and-seventy wins and losses apiece with the Silver Boot tiebreaker in Houston's keeping. Texas also sits one game from Chicago's wild-card chair; the Maple Leaf nine slip two back with their candle guttering.

MAHLE CARVES SIX QUIET INNINGS AND THREE TWO-RUN THUNDERCLAPS DO THE REST — THE TOMAHAWK NINE SEAL AN EIGHTH OCTOBER IN NINE YEARS: TOMAHAWK NINE 6, ASTROS 2

Harris in the fourth, Acuña in the seventh, Olson in the ninth — each blow worth two runs, the last of them the fortieth the milestone desk celebrates — and Tyler Mahle made them stand with six innings of one run and six strikeouts on clinching night, as the October desk relates. Paredes drove in both Houston runs in a five-hit evening; the Astros have lost six of ten, and Friday's defeat dropped them into the .500 deadlock with Texas that now defines the West. Atlanta's East arithmetic — five up, a sweep-and-help scenario to clinch by Sunday — stands in the desk above.

CHOURIO'S OPENING STATEMENT, ALONSO'S ANSWER, AND A VERDICT DELIVERED IN THE TENTH — WIN SIX-AND-NINETY COMES THE HARD WAY: BREWERS 6, ORIOLES 5, IN TEN INNINGS

Jackson Chourio struck a three-run homer in the second and stole two bases besides — one theft shy now of a third consecutive twenty-twenty season — and Pete Alonso answered with a three-run blow of his own, upheld by the machines, for his eight-and-thirtieth. Milwaukee took the lead back in the ninth on Contreras' double and Yelich's single, watched Baltimore square it with two sacrifice flies off Megill — his first blown save since the fifth of June — and settled the matter in the tenth on Frelick's single, Patrick sealing it. Victory six-and-ninety stands one shy of the franchise record set only last season, and the bye arithmetic reads three, as the October desk counts.

THREE RUNS OFF THE OPENER BEFORE AN OUT WAS BOUGHT, THREE MORE FROM SOTO'S BAT — THE AMAZINS PULL PHILADELPHIA BACK INTO THE PACK: AMAZINS 6, PHILADELPHIAS 3

The opener Mayza surrendered three runs in a third of an inning, and the newly claimed José Urquidy — the waiver prize of Thursday's dealings desk — gave four and two-thirds scoreless with six strikeouts in a debut that deserved better company. Sosa's homer and double clawed Philadelphia within one before Juan Soto turned on Kerkering for a three-run homer, his six-and-twentieth, and Hill's eleventh closed the account. The defeat drops the Philadelphias into the three-way dead heat the October desk describes, five behind Atlanta in the East; the Amazins, long since out of the argument, collected thirteen hits and looked pleased with the spoiler's wages.

SKENES IS REACHED FOR FIVE AND THE SMOKY CITY NINE RALLY ROUND HIM — GRIFFIN'S FOUR HITS AND A THREE-RUN SEVENTH RESTORE THE LEDGER TO .500: SMOKY CITY NINE 8, ROYALS 5

Pasquantino and Massey both took Paul Skenes out of the yard, and the great arm left after six trailing — whereupon his mates paid the debt: Konnor Griffin collected four hits and two runs driven in, Lowe hammered his two-and-thirtieth with a man aboard, and a three-run seventh off Pearson — Horwitz singling home two, Griffin one — turned the evening for good. Ramírez took the decision, Soto sealed his fifteenth save, and Pittsburgh stands at seven-and-seventy wins and defeats alike, a .500 figure worn like a pressed suit in a lost year.

THE ACE IN MID-NEGOTIATION STATES HIS PRICE FROM THE MOUND — FIVE SCORELESS FROM CAVALLI AND SEVEN RUNS IN THREE INNINGS: SENATORS 9, CARDINALS 1

Cade Cavalli, whose contract-extension talks this paper entered only yesterday, argued his side of the table with five scoreless innings and six strikeouts for his thirteenth victory — a well-timed exhibit if ever the wires saw one. Dylan Crews' two-run homer crowned a seven-run burst across the first three innings off Leahy, and Washington cruised behind four doubles besides. St. Louis managed Herrera's late run and little else, a third straight defeat; Burleson went hitless, though his hundred eleven driven in still lead the National's ledger.

FIVE WALKS COME HOME TO ROOST IN A THREE-RUN SIXTH — HOLMES UNRAVELS AT CINCINNATI, AND THE BRUINS ARE PULLED BACK INTO THE DEAD HEAT: CINCINNATIS 6, BRUINS 4

Chicago led by a run behind Suzuki's two-run single and Happ's four-and-twentieth, but Clay Holmes walked five men through five and a third, and the sixth inning collected the arrears: Suárez singled the game level and Trevino lined a two-run knock for the lead, the freshly recalled Aguiar taking the decision and Pagán sealing his four-and-twentieth. The defeat, paired with Philadelphia's and San Diego's evening, closes the National's wild-card row into the three-way deadlock the October desk describes — the Bruins' cushion, a game and a half at Thursday's dawn, now vanished entirely.

A SIX-RUN FIFTH BOUNCES OFF THE MOUND AND INTO THE WESTERN METAL BUILDING — ELEVEN WINS IN TWELVE FOR THE SAN DIEGO NINE: SAN DIEGO NINE 8, GULF STREAM NINE 2

The go-ahead blow was Dustin Harris' single that caromed off the mound itself, and the exclamation was Ty France's towering three-run homer off the Western Metal Building — the heart of a six-run fifth — before Merrill's six-and-twentieth arrived in the eighth with a kiss planted on the barrel of his bat. Pivetta gave five innings of one for the victory. Eleven wins in twelve have carried the San Diego nine dead level with the Cubs and Phillies at the row's head, five clear of Arizona, with a clinch possible as soon as tomorrow; the Gulf Stream nine took their ten hits home for consolation.

FIVE IN THE FIRST WITHOUT THE CAPTAIN, AND COLE PASSES EVERY FIRST PICK BEFORE HIM — THE BRONX BOMBERS GAIN A GAME ON TAMPA BAY: BRONX BOMBERS 9, SNAKES 2

Hours after the calf verdict the ward above records, New York answered in the oldest dialect it knows: five runs in the first off Rodriguez, the fifteen-game winner, with Ben Rice walking one home before adding his team-leading nine-and-thirtieth homer and a triple, and the young George Lombard Jr. driving in three. Gerrit Cole gave six innings of two for the one hundred two-and-sixtieth victory of his career — passing Mike Moore for the most ever gathered by a first-overall draft selection — and the Bombers, winners of eleven in fifteen, drew within four of Tampa Bay before Tuesday's four-game reckoning. Carroll's two-and-twentieth was the whole of Arizona's answer; a third straight defeat leaves the Snakes five from the last chair with eight to play.

FIFTEEN HITS GO FOR NOTHING IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR — MONTES' NINTH-INNING THUNDER STEALS IT FOR THE PUGET SOUND MEN: PUGET SOUND MEN 5, MILE HIGH NINE 4

Seattle's early three — Crawford's homer on the game's first swing of consequence and Naylor's two-run single — were run down by degrees, McCarthy tripling and singling twice among Colorado's fifteen hits, and the Mile High nine led by the sixth. But Canzone's sacrifice fly squared it in the seventh, and in the ninth Lazaro Montes struck his fourth homer for the lead, Muñoz sealing the eight-and-twentieth save. It is a ninety-eighth defeat for Denver's men against a lone victory in their last ten — the arithmetic of a season now measured chiefly in patience.

SEVEN SPOTLESS INNINGS FROM PRIELIPP AND THE BOY JENKINS THUNDERS AGAIN — A WHITEWASH AT ANAHEIM: TWINS 3, ANGELS 0

Connor Prielipp gave the finest account of the evening's pitchers — seven scoreless innings, two hits, eight strikeouts — and Minnesota's three arrived by sacrifice fly, Bell's single, and Walker Jenkins' third home run, the youngster's second thunder in as many nights at the same address, his ninth-inning blow of Thursday having been entered in yesterday's card. Adams closed the four-hitter for his third save. The Angels, blanked, have now dropped five-and-ninety games; the same clubs resume this evening.

TWENTY YEARS TO THE NIGHT OF THE '4+1,' FOUR HOMERS IN A SINGLE INNING — BETTS STRIKES TWICE AND THE BOYS IN BLUE ROUT THE ORANGE AND BLACK: BOYS IN BLUE 8, ORANGE AND BLACK 2

Friday marked twenty years to the day since the '4+1' game of 2006, when four consecutive ninth-inning homers and Garciaparra's tenth-inning blow beat San Diego — and the champions honored the anniversary in kind, striking four home runs in the eighth inning alone: Muncy, Tucker, Mookie Betts with his second of the night, and Smith, in an evening begun with Betts' first-inning blow. Tyler Glasnow fanned ten across six innings for the victory, Díaz closed it in the return the convalescent desk sings, and all of it came without Ohtani. Lee's tenth homer and Cox's single made San Francisco's account, its shelved Webb entered in the ward above; the Boys in Blue hold four clear of Atlanta for the National's second seed, two behind Milwaukee.

The Saturday tables, then — with Atlanta's ticket punched and the captain of the Yankees on the shelf. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by four over clinched New York, Boston nine and a half astern; the Central is Cleveland's by one over Chicago, the tiebreaker still Chicago's, as the lead columns relate; and the West is a dead heat at last, Houston and Texas level at seven-and-seventy wins and losses apiece, the Silver Boot tiebreaker in Houston's keeping. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated in comfort, the last chair Chicago's by one over Texas, with Toronto two back and Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta, berth in pocket, leads Philadelphia by five; crowned Milwaukee by eleven over Chicago; the crowned champions by nine over San Diego. And the wild-card ledger is the morning's marvel: Cubs, Phillies, and Padres level to the game at five-and-eighty wins and nine-and-sixty defeats — three clubs, three chairs, the order a matter of tiebreakers alone, San Diego seated third — with Arizona five back and eight to play. Today's bill is the full board of fifteen, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends: at 2:10 daylight baseball on the South Side, where Detroit and Chicago resume their argument, Jobe opposing Burke; at 4:10 Boston tries for the formal seating at Tampa Bay, where a berth may be sealed by evening, other scoreboards consenting; at 7:05 Soriano carries Toronto's thinning case against Quantrill at Arlington; at 8:10 Schlittler — fourteen victories and the American's best earned-run figure at 1.95 — takes the Yankee cause into Phoenix without the captain; and at 9:10 Skubal opposes the Orange and Black at Chavez Ravine. Eight mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

entry.title: THE CORONATION, POSTPONED A NIGHT, ARRIVES BY BULLPEN PARADE — A THIRTEENTH WEST FLAG IN FOURTEEN YEARS IS SEWN ON AT CINCINNATI: DODGERS 8, REDS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 72 · Friday, the Eighteenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 9 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE CORONATION, POSTPONED A NIGHT, ARRIVES BY BULLPEN PARADE — A THIRTEENTH WEST FLAG IN FOURTEEN YEARS IS SEWN ON AT CINCINNATI: DODGERS 8, REDS 2

Tucker strikes four blows and finishes a triple shy of the club's first cycle since 2017; Knack, summoned from Oklahoma City that very morning, banks four scoreless innings for the victory; and the champions' fourteenth consecutive October now aims itself at a prize no club has taken thrice running since the century turned

The champagne had waited a night in its ice, and the champions elected not to make it wait a second. Denied on Wednesday when Snell's groin gave way after an inning — as this paper recorded yesterday, coronation postponed — the Dodgers came to Thursday afternoon at Cincinnati with a patchwork bullpen day where a starter ought to have been, and turned it into a procession. Justin Wrobleski opened with three perfect innings; Landon Knack, recalled from Oklahoma City only that morning, gave four scoreless in the middle for the victory; and by the time Halvorsen surrendered a courtesy run in the ninth the score stood 8-2, the West stood clinched, and the visiting clubhouse stood ankle-deep in its second champagne of the week — the berth toasted Monday, the flag properly celebrated now.

The day's largest bat belonged to Kyle Tucker: four hits in five tries, a two-run homer in the first, doubles in the second and fourth, three runs driven, and a ninth-inning at-bat that came up one triple shy of the club's first cycle since 2017. Freeman, Muncy, De Paula, and Rojas all drove in runs behind him — Muncy's a two-run double in the three-run fourth, Rojas' a solo homer in the ninth — while Cincinnati's answer was confined to Stewart's two-and-thirtieth home run, struck off Treinen in the fourth. Singer absorbed the loss, seven runs in three and a third.

The ledger of the dynasty asks a moment's awe. This is the thirteenth division title in fourteen years — only the 2021 Giants ever interrupted — the fifth in succession, and the fourteenth consecutive October engagement; since divisional play began in 1969 no club has gathered more such flags than Los Angeles' four-and-twenty, one clear of Atlanta. "You get so mired in each year, it's hard to have any perspective," said the president Friedman. "But the important thing is how we finish and how we go into October." The manager Roberts stated the house terms plainly: "If you don't win the World Series, you fail. But that's kind of part of what you signed up with the Dodgers." What they chase now is the game's first three-peat since the 1998-2000 Yankees — pursued, it must be said, at less than full strength, with Ohtani and Pages both on the invalid list, Snell's groin under watch, and the six-man rotation of summer reduced to four stretched arms. "We've had guys go down. We've had guys step up in their place," shrugged Muncy. "We've been able to survive a lot." Betts put the creed shortest: "Getting here, you can't really get too focused on how, as long as you get there."

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: A TERRIFYING MINUTE AT FLUSHING — JARED YOUNG CARTED OFF AFTER A COLLISION AT FIRST BASE, AND THE HOSPITAL'S FIRST WORD IS GUARDEDLY GOOD; BOSTON'S CATCHER AND CLOSER BOTH DAY-TO-DAY

The ward's gravest entry stopped a ballgame cold. In the sixth inning at Citi Field, Philadelphia's Crawford tapped a slow roller toward first; the Mets' Jared Young and his pitcher McLean converged upon it, and McLean's knee struck Young's head at a full run. Young lay motionless while the trainers worked, then was carted from the field — a thumbs-up to the crowd as he went, consciousness regained — and taken to hospital, where the scan of his head came back negative. He showed concussion symptoms through the evening but full use of his limbs, and the interim manager Green pronounced the club optimistic he has "avoided the scariest outcomes." "That was a terrifying moment on a baseball field," Green said; the shortstop Lindor spoke for the room: "Life is bigger than this game, for sure." McLean, shaken, finished the inning — Green confessed afterward he regretted allowing even that — and asked to be excused from the pressmen. The Herald sets down its scorecard a moment and wishes the man a full and unhurried recovery.

The lesser cots are Boston's, and they matter to a pennant race. Willson Contreras took a pitch on the right hand in the eighth at Arlington and left the game; the X-rays came back negative, the diagnosis a bruise with swelling, the prognosis day-to-day. Aroldis Chapman, the closer, was unavailable altogether with tightness of the lat and is likewise day-to-day — "We're going to be conservative with it," said the interim manager Tracy. Both absences hang over a weekend at Tampa Bay that could seat Boston at October's table, as the desk below relates.

THE MOST-VALUABLE DESK: FORTY FOR ALVAREZ, ONE-AND-FORTY FOR CAMINERO — THE AMERICAN'S GREAT ARGUMENT SHARPENS, AND ITS BATTING RACE COMES DOWN TO SEVEN TEN-THOUSANDTHS

The American League's autumn argument gained a chapter on each coast of the Gulf. At Houston, Yordan Alvarez struck his fortieth home run — one of five separate Astro thunderclaps, as the card below records — and the wires promptly asked whether the Most Valuable canvass has become a two-man affair between Alvarez and Tampa Bay's Junior Caminero, who stands at one-and-forty homers with an .895 figure of on-base-and-slugging. "Not so fast," came the answer from Alvarez's own manager Espada and his teammates, who would widen the field; the Herald reminds the reader in any case that the writers' ballot is cast after the season and announced in November, and until then the argument is an argument, not an award.

Caminero, for his part, spent Thursday demonstrating that a man may carry a pennant race lightly. Chasing a foul ball to the Athletics' bullpen down the left-field line, he was met by the opposing reliever Medina bearing a cup of water; the third baseman drank it, tossed the cup, and jogged back to his station. "Hydration," he explained. "It's a long walk. That's my game right there — getting funny."

And beneath the home-run question runs a finer one: the batting race. Houston's Alvarez holds the American's lead at .3114; Tampa Bay's Chandler Simpson — two hits Thursday, his five-and-fiftieth multi-hit game, batting .356 across three months — sits at .3107, seven ten-thousandths behind, with his four-and-fortieth stolen base banked besides. "I know he hates to talk about numbers; I'll talk about them for him," said his teammate Palacios. Nine days remain for the decimals to argue.

THE DEALINGS DESK: A WAIVER PRIZE CROSSES THE LEAGUE LINE — URQUIDY TO PHILADELPHIA, AND WASHINGTON OPENS ITS PURSE TOWARD ITS ACE

Philadelphia, arranging its October pantry, claimed the right-hander José Urquidy off waivers from the White Sox on Thursday — a veteran arm with a champion's pedigree from his Houston years, acquired for the price of a claim. To clear the room, the Phillies moved the right-hander Kilian to the sixty-day shelf with his oblique strain. The Quaker City's rotation ledger explains the appetite: Luzardo on the shelf, as this paper recorded Wednesday, and every contender in the National hunting insurance arms for the rounds ahead.

In Washington, meanwhile, the wires report the Nationals in contract-extension talks with their ace, the right-hander Cade Cavalli — per a source, the club not yet confirming. The case for haste writes itself: eight-and-twenty years old, twelve victories against five defeats with an earned-run figure of 3.12, under contract until 2030 but pitching this season like a man whose price rises by the start. He takes the ball this very night at St. Louis; the purse and the pitcher will presumably keep talking.

THE OCTOBER DESK: ARLINGTON STAGES THE WEEKEND'S HEAVYWEIGHT BILL — TWO CLUBS DEAD LEVEL AT SIX-AND-SEVENTY WINS, WITH THE WEST AND THE LAST CHAIRS ALIKE IN THE BALANCE

With nine days left to the season's final page, the schedule-makers have delivered their best card to Texas: the Blue Jays and Rangers, each at six-and-seventy wins and seven-and-seventy defeats, open three games at Arlington tonight with consequences running in every direction — the American's West, where Thursday's defeat dropped Texas a game behind Houston, and the wild-card row, where both clubs sit two games from the last chair with the tiebreakers and the arithmetic all still in motion. Toronto sends its ace Cease, he of the 2.38 earned-run figure and the American's strikeout lead, against Rocker in the opener; the loser of the series may find the mathematics turned suddenly cruel.

The weekend's other appointments carry their own October freight. Boston, holder of the second wild-card chair, calls at Tampa Bay with a chance to seat itself formally at the table — the Red Sox can clinch a postseason berth at the Trop this very weekend, catcher and closer permitting, as the ward above frets. Atlanta, the East's leader, opens at Houston, where the newly throned West leaders wait; and the crowned Brewers call at Baltimore still hunting victory six-and-ninety. The desk commends the whole card to the reader's lamp-oil.

The Rest of the Card

DOWN THREE BY THE SECOND, AND ONE SWING REWRITES THE EVENING — STORY'S FIRST THUNDER SINCE MAY ARRIVES THREE RUNS DEEP, AND A 72-AND-1 LEDGER TAKES ITS SECOND BLOT: BOSTONS 4, LONE STAR NINE 3

Texas entered the night two-and-seventy wins against a single defeat when leading in the eighth inning or later; it left with the second. Down 3-0 from the second inning — Jung's homer and a squeeze among the damage — Boston scratched one back in the seventh, then put two aboard in the eighth on Abreu's walk and the hit batsman that sent Contreras to the ward above before Trevor Story turned on an eighty-mile curveball from Latz and lined it to left-center: a three-run blow, his first home run since the thirteenth of May and fourth of the year, on the far side of surgery and three lost months. "That was the point of getting the surgery — to come back and try to be the player that I know I can be," said Story, riding an eight-game hitting streak. Gray gave six and a third of three-run ball on a season-high one hundred two pitches, Whitlock sealed the fourth save, and Boston — its sweep averted, its second wild-card chair held five clear — set off for Tampa with clinching on its mind. Texas fell a game behind Houston in the West, its wounds catalogued in the desk above.

FIVE SEPARATE THUNDERCLAPS, THE FORTIETH AMONG THEM — THE HOUSTON NINE TAKE THE WEST'S THRONE ALONE: HOUSTON NINE 6, ROYAL BLUES 2

A day after sharing the summit, Houston claimed it outright by the simplest means the game allows: five home runs from five different men. Peña's twentieth answered Kansas City's early run in the first, Varsho's twelfth followed in the second, and the fifth inning brought Wade Jr.'s fourth and then Yordan Alvarez's fortieth — the blow that feeds the Most Valuable argument above — before Trammell, activated from the paternity list only that morning, added the eighth of his year in the eighth inning. Lugo surrendered four of the five and the loss; the rookie Pecko gave five and two-thirds of one-run relief behind the opener. Kansas City managed three hits, two of them Jensen's. The Houston nine lead Texas by a game with nine to play, and Atlanta arrives tonight.

MURAKAMI'S THREE-RUN STATEMENT STANDS ALL NIGHT, AND THE PROPHECY OF YESTERDAY'S COLUMNS IS KEPT — A SHARE OF THE THRONE RETAKEN WITHOUT CLEVELAND THROWING A PITCH: SOUTH SIDERS 3, DETROITS 1

This paper observed only yesterday that Chicago might retake a share of the Central without Cleveland lifting a finger, the new leaders being idle; the South Siders required three batters to set about it. Munetaka Murakami struck a three-run homer in the first — his two-and-thirtieth, with Meidroth and Grichuk aboard — later added a triple, and the three runs stood untouched to the end. Fedde carved six strikeouts into the fifth, Hudson took the decision, Taylor banked a seven-out save, and the third baseman Vargas twice robbed Detroit with the glove at moments the wires called crucial. The ledger this morning: Chicago and Cleveland level at eight-and-seventy wins apiece, the tiebreaker Chicago's, banked Monday, as these columns have thrice recorded — meaning the Cleveland nine must still finish clear. Detroit has dropped two straight since its six-game surge.

A TWO-OUT WALK, THEN SEVEN STRAIGHT CORSAIRS ABOARD — THE AUDITION ENDS IN THE SECOND INNING, AND MILWAUKEE'S SIX-AND-NINETIETH MUST WAIT: CORSAIRS 7, MILWAUKEES 4

The audition this paper flagged yesterday came to order at PNC Park and adjourned inside two innings. Kyle Harrison, auditioning for an October role, walked Simon with two out in the second and watched seven consecutive Pirates reach — Griffin's two-run double, Cruz's two-run single, and Lowe's hit-by-pitch with the bases full among the wreckage — before departing at five runs, his figure across the last four outings now a grim 21.00. "I'm not going to give in, not going to give up," the left-hander vowed, and his manager Murphy kept a door ajar: "We're not giving up hope that he's going to be really effective for us soon." Davis' two-run homer in the eighth answered Naylor's review-upheld blow for Milwaukee, and Montgomery sealed the fourteenth save. The crowned Milwaukees, stalled at five-and-ninety wins, carry the hundred-win arithmetic to Baltimore tonight.

SIX IN THE FOURTH, A SIXTEENTH SWEEP, AND THE RETURNING SHORTSTOP BUNTS HIS WAY INTO THE LEDGER: GULF COAST CLUB 10, MACKMEN 1

The sweep this paper's Thursday columns saw the Gulf Coast club attempting is banked — a sixteenth of the season, extending the franchise record, the most by any club since the 2022 Dodgers — on the strength of a six-run fourth: Simpson's two-run single, Palacios' two-run double with Vilade scampering home on the loose throw, and Taylor Walls, activated from the shelf that very morning, dropping a perfect bunt single along the third-base line for the sixth run of the frame. The bunt was the club's seven-and-fortieth hit of the kind this year, the second-most of any team since such things were tracked. Rasmussen coasted five scoreless for his fifteenth victory — the Rays have now won eleven straight games he has started, tying the franchise record set across Matt Moore's 2012-13 turns — and the winning streak stands at six, the East's lead at five, with Boston arriving tonight. Butler's homer spared the Mackmen the shutout.

A SEVEN-RUN SECOND, THREE TRIPLES IN ONE AFTERNOON, AND BOGAERTS COMES A SINGLE SHY OF THE CYCLE — THE MISSION NINE BANK A TENTH IN ELEVEN: MISSION NINE 9, COLORADANS 2

Xander Bogaerts did the hard parts first — a homer leading off the second, a triple to cap the seven-run rally that followed as San Diego batted around, a double off the left-center wall in the fourth — and then chased the humble single in vain to the last. "I wanted it bad," he admitted. The Mission nine struck fifteen hits in all, three of them triples (Merrill and Cronenworth joining the fun), Harris driving in three; King gave six innings of two for his twelfth victory. The arithmetic travels well: ten victories in eleven games, a road trip closed at six wins and one defeat, and the third wild-card chair now held by four full games over Arizona with the season's final series against those very Snakes still waiting at Petco. Denver's misery deepens at six-and-fifty wins.

SEVEN SPOTLESS INNINGS IN THE OLD STYLE — NOLA BLANKS THE METROPOLITANS ON A NIGHT THE GAME ITSELF STOOD STILL: BROTHERLY LOVE NINE 3, METROPOLITANS 0

Aaron Nola threw seven scoreless innings of three hits — vintage stuff, the wires calling this run his best since 2018 — and Philadelphia manufactured its three runs the artisan's way: Harper's challenge-overturned single in the fifth, then sacrifice flies from Arraez and Crawford in the seventh and eighth. Harper collected three hits, Duran sealed his two-and-thirtieth save, and the Brotherly Love nine opened at Flushing with a second straight victory to stay level with the Cubs atop the wild-card row, four behind Atlanta in the East. The Metropolitans, blanked on four hits, have lost five running — and their evening's true weight was carried off on a cart in the sixth, as the ward above records with the whole game's good wishes.

SEVEN SCORELESS FROM THE ROOKIE UREÑA, TWO MINNESOTA RALLIES, AND MECKLER'S SINGLE ENDS IT IN THE TENTH: HALOS 5, MINNESOTANS 4

The rookie Walbert Ureña gave the finest turn of his young year — seven scoreless innings, nine strikeouts, not a walk — and then watched his 3-0 lead nearly come to grief twice over. Minnesota's Jenkins, hitting but .143 on the year, scored on Lee's sacrifice fly in the eighth and tied the game himself with a two-run homer in the ninth; Lee's single in the tenth put the visitors ahead. But the last of the tenth belonged to Anaheim: Mike Trout lined the tying run home, and Meckler — two hits on the night — grounded the winner through the right side. The Minnesotans struck out fifteen times in defeat and get the same hosts again tonight; the Halos, long since out of the argument, keep collecting evenings worth the gate.

The Friday tables, then — with the champions' flag of the West newly sewn on. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by five over clinched New York, Boston ten and a half astern; the Central is a dead heat once more, Chicago and Cleveland level at eight-and-seventy wins with the tiebreaker Chicago's; and the West is Houston's by one over Texas, the Silver Boot insurance still in Houston's keeping. The wild-card row: New York and Boston seated in comfort, the last chair Cleveland's, with Texas and Toronto two back — tonight's antagonists at Arlington, as the October desk sings — and Baltimore three. In the National: Atlanta by four over Philadelphia; crowned Milwaukee by ten over Chicago; crowned Los Angeles by nine over San Diego. The wild-card ledger: the Cubs and Phillies level at the row's head, San Diego in the third chair by four over Arizona, Miami and Pittsburgh eight back and dimming. Tonight's bill is a full fifteen engagements, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends: at 7:10 Boston opens at the Trop with a berth there for the clinching, Seymour opposing Suarez; at 8:05 Cease carries Toronto's case into Arlington against Rocker, with the West and the last chairs alike at hazard; at 8:10 Atlanta calls upon newly throned Houston; and at 9:40 the Yankees open at Phoenix against Rodriguez, fifteen victories and a 2.62 figure to his name. Nine mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~

The Herald Acknowledges Its Debts

entry.title: THE UNDERSTUDY BRINGS DOWN THE HOUSE — HALPIN'S THREE-RUN THUNDER TURNS THE SUMMIT'S FINAL ACT, AND CLEVELAND STANDS ALONE ATOP THE CENTRAL FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE INDEPENDENCE DAY: GUARDIANS 6, WHITE SOX 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 71 · Thursday, the Seventeenth of September, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE UNDERSTUDY BRINGS DOWN THE HOUSE — HALPIN'S THREE-RUN THUNDER TURNS THE SUMMIT'S FINAL ACT, AND CLEVELAND STANDS ALONE ATOP THE CENTRAL FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE INDEPENDENCE DAY: GUARDIANS 6, WHITE SOX 3

Pressed into center field only because the ward had emptied it, Petey Halpin answers Pham's return-day blow with the biggest swing of his life; Messick fans eight, one Smith loses what the other Smith seals, and the half-game lead changes uniforms with ten mornings left to run

For the first time since the morning of the Fourth of July, the top line of the American's Central reads Cleveland — and the swing that turned the column belonged to the one man in the building with no billing on the playbill. Petey Halpin, four-and-twenty years old, is a reserve outfielder by trade; he stood in center field yesterday afternoon only because the invalid list had claimed DeLauter and Martínez for a second consecutive day. In the sixth, his club down a run, Fry and Hedges walked ahead of him and the left-hander Newcomb summoned to face him, Halpin took a 3-1 sinker that its author later confessed was "just middle" and struck it three-and-ninety feet past three hundred to right — a three-run blow, just the fourth hit of his major-league life off a southpaw, and by his own accounting the biggest swing of his baseball life. He tossed the bat aside, stared a long moment at his own dugout, and hop-stepped backward toward first while the park came down around him. "I knew I hit well off the bat," he deposed. "Having that moment and sharing it with the guys in a big game, a big series, it was really cool." In the dugout the winning pitcher confessed to assaulting the water cooler out of sheer joy; the manager Vogt put it plainer: "He's ready for the moment."

The ledger around the thunderbolt deserves its lines. Cleveland's first two runs were a gift of Chicago carpentry — the second baseman Meidroth dropped the tag on a double play that wasn't, in the third, and Adell cashed the mistake with a two-run single ("Maybe keep the other hand on the ball?" offered the Chicago manager Venable, a touch grimly). The visitors' answer was the day's second-best story: Tommy Pham, activated only that morning from the calf strain that had shelved him since the third of the month, struck a three-run homer measured at a dozen feet past four hundred — his first of the year — to put the Pale Hose ahead 3-2 in the fifth. It was the whole of the damage against Parker Messick, who gave six innings with eight strikeouts for his twelfth victory and whose name now rides both the Rookie of the Year and Cy Young ballots-to-come. Ramírez's second double of the afternoon — his first extra-base hits of the month — made it 6-3, and the ninth resolved into the connoisseur's curiosity: the loss charged to Chicago's Smith, the save banked by Cleveland's, the seven-and-thirtieth of Cade Smith's year. "Coming into this series, it was a playoff game for every person that walked into this building," said Messick, and no one in either clubhouse argued.

Now the arithmetic, which is the morning's true headline. Cleveland leads by half a game — but the tiebreaker remains Chicago's, banked Monday as this paper has twice recorded, so the Cleveland nine must finish clear, not level. Nine games remain to them, ten to Chicago, and the road ahead is gentler for the deposed on paper — Tigers, Royals, and Rockies for Chicago, against Cleveland's Athletics, Red Sox, and Royals. The victory also lifts Cleveland a game and a half clear of the West's deadlocked co-leaders for the American's second seed and the first-round bye that rides with it. And tonight offers the strangest wrinkle of all: Chicago hosts Detroit while Cleveland sits idle, an evening on which the deposed can retake a share of the throne without their rival throwing a pitch. "Giving up the division lead, everybody will feel how they feel about it," said Venable. "But I'm proud of the guys and I think we're in a good spot moving forward." Vogt, whose club stands seven-and-seventy wins against seven-and-forty defeats in Septembers since 2022, declined the laurel: "It feels good. It doesn't mean anything yet, right? We've got a job to do for nine more games." The desk has called this fixture the week's own since Monday; it now calls the Central what it has been all along — a coin standing on its edge.

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: JUDGE WALKS OFF IN THE SIXTH WITH A TIGHTENED LEG AND SNELL LASTS ONE INNING IN CINCINNATI — TWO PILLARS OF OCTOBER VISIT THE EXAMINING TABLE IN A SINGLE EVENING

The ward's gravest pair arrived within hours of one another. In Minneapolis, Aaron Judge — restored to the Yankee lineup barely a week from three months lost to the fractured rib — felt a stiffness in the lower right leg from the first inning, struck out twice, and was lifted for a pinch-hitter in the sixth of what became the thirteen-inning defeat the card below records. "I tried to kind of play it off and see how long we could go, because these games are important down the stretch," the great man said, "but I thought it'd be the right move to come out." He anticipates no testing; the club will pour two days of treatment into the Thursday off-day and say nothing sooner. "We're not going to speculate one way or the other," said the manager Boone. "We'll just see how he responds."

In Cincinnati the champions' evening went sideways on the second-to-last pitch of a bullpen warm-up. Blake Snell felt the left groin grab, tried the first inning anyway — nineteen pitches, his fastball down a mile and a half — and reported himself to the trainers rather than test a muscle he has strained four times before. "For me to stop, that's a first. Maybe I'm growing up," said the lefty, who had been untouchable since August, four victories and an earned-run figure of 1.04 across six starts. The manager Roberts filed it under "glad it's not worse," but the stakes need no embroidery: "He just can't afford any more setbacks. We've got to make sure that he comes out ready to go in the postseason." The defeat also postponed the West's coronation, as the card relates.

The lesser cots: in Texas, the Rangers' starter Gore fought muscle spasms through four laboring innings — nine-and-sixty pitches, six-and-thirty strikes — before yielding to the extraordinary relief the card below sings; Baltimore's Jackson Holliday went to the ten-day list with inflammation of the left wrist, his replacement answering in the manner the card describes; and Chicago's Montgomery left the summit's finale with a bruised left wrist from a Messick pitch, though the X-rays came back clean and the man is called day-to-day. The ward keeps its lamps trimmed.

THE MILESTONE DESK: TWENTY YEARS AND ONE HUNDRED SEVEN DAYS OLD, AND NO CATCHER SO YOUNG HAS EVER STRUCK TWO IN A GAME — ETHAN SALAS OPENS HIS CAREER'S ACCOUNT WITH BOTH BARRELS IN THE MOUNTAIN AIR

The first home run of Ethan Salas' major-league life left Coors Field at a measured six-and-twenty feet past four hundred, dead to center, on the first pitch he saw in the second inning. The second left three innings later. At twenty years and one hundred seven days, the Padres' boy catcher thereby became the youngest man ever to catch a big-league game and strike two home runs in it — the youngest Padre at any position to do so, the youngest to homer as a catcher since Iván Rodríguez in September of 1991, and the youngest player of any station with a multi-homer game since Guerrero the younger in 2019. The roll of those who managed it younger in the past twenty years reads Trout, Harper, Soto, and one Manny Machado, who now dresses in the same room. "I'm just a kid playing baseball, man," Salas said. "So it's pretty crazy to be in company with such high-caliber guys like that."

The account had opened slowly — hitless in his first fifteen at-bats before Sunday's triple at San Francisco loosened the hinge — but the club promoted him for the glove, not the barrel, and the glove did its own day's work: a shrewd challenge of the machines ended the first inning with two Rockies stranded, and the veteran Ray, throwing to him for the first time, gave six tidy innings and pronounced him "great back there." The manager Stammen took the wider view: "Playing the position that he plays, it makes it doubly tough. He's got a lot thrown at him — and then: 'Oh yeah, you're expected to hit, too.'" The evening's consequences for the pennant arithmetic stand in the card below; the desk here records only that the youngest catcher in five-and-thirty years spent his history-making night grinning like exactly what he claims to be.

THE CLUBHOUSE DESK: TWO DAYS AFTER THROWING ONE HUNDRED ONE PITCHES, THE ACE OF MIAMI ASKS FOR THE NINTH — ALCANTARA'S FIRST SAVE IN NINE SEASONS SENDS THE LAUNDRY CART ROLLING

The manager knew before the game; the starter Gusto pieced it together when he saw the big man lacing his cleats in full uniform in the sixth inning; the rest of the world found out when Sandy Alcantara — one hundred one pitches in Monday's series opener, a single day of rest behind him — strode out of the Miami bullpen to protect a one-run lead in the ninth at Phoenix. Two flyouts, a walk, and a caught-stealing later, the face of the Marlins franchise owned the first save of his nine-season life. He had asked the pitching coach for the assignment before the game, with the closer Fairbanks and the setup man Bender both lost for the year and the bullpen freshly emptied. "I want to die out there for my team," Alcantara said. "That's why I'm here. Every time they give me this opportunity, I will take it."

The wires supply the genealogy: since the save became an official statistic in 1969, only three other men had recorded one on a day they entered leading — or sharing the lead in — all the major leagues in innings pitched: Hershiser in '87, Niekro in '78, Messersmith in '75. Alcantara makes four. The clubhouse afterward gave its stoic ace the rookie's rite — the laundry-cart ride into the showers, beer and shaving cream attending — and the man permitted it, which those who know him rank among the evening's larger surprises. "The dude is an inspiration," said Gusto. "I can't even explain how fired up we were." Even the beaten manager Lovullo tipped a puzzled cap: "That's an elite arm, an elite starting pitcher. I was a little bit confused — but to each their own. They won the baseball game." Miami sits seven and a half from the National's last chair with nine to play, mathematically distant and temperamentally unbeaten.

THE OCTOBER DESK: THE CONTENDERS BEGIN ARRANGING THEIR PIECES — ATLANTA RESTS SALE FOR A WILD-CARD OPENER NOT YET EARNED, AND CROWNED MILWAUKEE GOES HUNTING ROUND NUMBERS

The month's endgame has begun on the blackboards as well as the field. Atlanta — leading the East by four and a half with a magic number of five, the earliest clinching possible Saturday — will not pitch Chris Sale in this weekend's Houston series at all, carrying him instead on six extra days' rest to a final regular-season turn Wednesday against Cincinnati, which in turn sets him up to open a Wild Card series on a rested arm. The ledger justifies the indulgence: the ancient left-hander has made but two starts on regular rest all year and owns a 1.98 earned-run figure across the three-and-twenty starts since the last of them. "It's a little bit of an extended break," allowed the manager Weiss, "but we feel it sets him up for the postseason." The thinness behind him is the worry — López to the shelf, as this paper recorded Tuesday, and the rookie Ritchie schooled at Wrigley in the manner the card below describes.

Milwaukee, its fourth straight Central crown one day old, celebrated by winning again — the particulars stand in the card — and awoke this morning at five-and-ninety victories, two shy of the club's best figure ever, with plain .500 ball across the last ten making the Central's first hundred-win outfit since the 2016 Cubs. The manager Murphy is husbanding arms rather than chasing numbers: Misiorowski was capped at two-and-eighty pitches Tuesday, Henderson at seven-and-eighty last night — his two-and-twentieth consecutive start of three runs or fewer to open a career — and the slumping Harrison auditions for an October role in this very afternoon's finale at Pittsburgh. "We've got work to do," said Murphy, and his closer Megill translated: "We're not resting people. We're playing tooth and nail. I would probably expect nothing less."

THE ALMANAC DESK: THIRTY YEARS AGO THIS VERY NIGHT, THE TORNADO TOUCHED DOWN AT COORS FIELD — NOMO'S NO-HITTER IN THE ONE PARK WHERE NO-HITTERS DO NOT HAPPEN

The almanac asks the reader to set down the standings a moment and mark an anniversary: on the seventeenth of September, 1996 — thirty years ago to this morning's date — Hideo Nomo of the Dodgers threw a no-hitter at Coors Field, the mile-high batting paradise where the great Scully himself had reckoned the feat "impossible." It remains singular: in the near four thousand eight hundred games played at that address since, no man has matched it. The night itself was all improbability — a two-hour rain delay, a cold drizzle, and the whirling "Tornado" windup abandoned for the stretch, out of which the enigmatic right-hander from Japan spun the forkball his old pitching coach Wallace still calls "really two pitches — he would throw it for a called strike and then he'd get a chase." Bichette, the previous year's runner-up for Most Valuable, struck out against it three times. "Those Rockies never saw a split-finger like he threw," says Candiotti, who watched from the same dugout. "These guys now, there are guys with good splitters. But they're not like Nomo's. Not even close. Unreal."

The wires append the desk's favorite grace note, from the man's very debut the year before: mound conference, bases loaded, hundreds of Japanese pressmen watching, and the pitching coach — out of pure instinct — asking his new charge "¿Cómo está?" ("Hey Dave," the catcher Piazza observed, "he's Japanese, not Spanish.") Nomo nodded, answered "Good," and struck the next man out. Thirty years on, with last night's Coors card entry full of a teenager's thunder as the milestone desk sings, the Herald lifts its cap to the night the impossible park stood silent.

THE PIONEER DESK: THE QUEENS DRAW FIRST BLOOD IN THE WOMEN'S LEAGUE CHAMPIONSHIP — MACKAY THROWS FIVE AND TWO-THIRDS FROM THE BULLPEN, AND MO'NE DAVIS SCORES THE TYING RUN

The reader will recall from yesterday's columns that Mo'ne Davis had come to St. Louis to watch her old Monarchs teammate wear a big-league uniform, her own championship business waiting just up the road; that business has now heard from her. In the first championship game the Women's Professional Baseball League has ever played, Davis' Los Angeles Queens beat the first-place San Francisco Firebells seven runs to six — and did it the hard way, down 6-2 after three innings with their starter gone four outs in. The rescue belonged to Jamie Mackay, a power-hitting catcher by trade who had never thrown more than three and two-thirds innings in an outing: she gave five and two-thirds from the bullpen, struck out five, and retired the final nine batters she faced. "I'll do anything to help our team," she said, which the box score renders redundant.

The rally's hinge was the desk's returning heroine: Davis led off the sixth with a double and came home with the tying run on the captain Lansdell's double inside the third-base bag, before the Australian captain Eynon — three singles in three tries already — lifted the go-ahead sacrifice fly. "Baseball is a big game of momentum," said Eynon, the game's named player. The Queens thus lead the best-of-five a game to none, with the second act on the league's bill for this very night. One sandlot in South Philadelphia, the Herald observes, has now furnished a big-league debut and a championship rally in the same week; the man who drags that infield should charge admission.

The Rest of the Card

SEVEN INNINGS OF SCORELESS COMMAND FROM WHEELER, THREE STRIKEOUTS SHY OF TWO THOUSAND — AND THIRTEEN WALKS DRAWN BESIDES: QUAKERS 3, CAPITAL NINE 0

Zack Wheeler gave seven scoreless innings of four hits, facing the minimum across his last three frames and closing his night by blowing a fastball past Crews — the 1,997th strikeout of his career. The Quakers drew thirteen walks off Washington's staff and still stranded thirteen men, Arraez walking thrice and doubling besides; Duran sealed his one-and-thirtieth save, and the Capital nine's four-game winning run, entered in yesterday's columns, is ended. Philadelphia sits half a game behind the Cubs at the head of the wild-card row, with the arithmetic in the October desk above.

FOUR HOME RUNS, A SWEEP OF FLUSHING, AND THE POLAR BEAR'S THREE HUNDRED FIRST — THE BALTIMORES REFUSE TO LEAVE THE RACE: BALTIMORES 7, METS 1

Pete Alonso opened the evening with a four-hundred-ten-foot blast into the second deck — career homer three hundred one, his seven-and-thirtieth of the year, cheered by the Flushing crowd for a third consecutive night — and Jackson, Encarnacion-Strand, and Basallo followed him out, the last pair back-to-back. Bassitt gave six and two-thirds of one-run ball for the sweep, and the Elias bureau notes the same three Baltimore hitters homered in consecutive games for the first time since Davis, Machado, and Trumbo in August of 2016. "Am I surprised that Pete does this? No, because he's literally that good," said Bassitt of his once-and-again teammate. The Baltimores have won three straight and sit two and a half from the American's last chair — alive, if breathing thin air — while Jackson's thunder covers the wrist-sore Holliday, as the ward above records.

THIRTEEN INNINGS IN THE DRIZZLE END ON CARATINI'S SINGLE — THE HIGHLANDERS SQUANDER A LOADED TWELFTH, AND THE GREAT MAN'S EXIT SHADOWS ALL: TWIN CITIES NINE 5, HIGHLANDERS 4

New York was down to its final out in the ninth when Volpe's double off the wall squared the account, and the clubs then traded single runs through the tenth and eleventh like duelists too tired to miss. The turn came in the twelfth — bases full of Highlanders, nobody out, and no runs to show for it, Ramos grounding into a double play with Volpe cut down at the plate — before Victor Caratini singled home Keaschall in the thirteenth to end it. The evening's asterisks: Judge's early exit fills the ward above; Schmidt, activated from his elbow reconstruction that very day — as this paper forecast Monday — threw his first innings of the year; and the pursuit of Tampa Bay stretches to four and a half with the Bronx idle today.

THREE TWO-OUT DOUBLES BEFORE THE FIRST INNING WAS OVER — THE SUNSHINE NINE BANK A FIFTH STRAIGHT AND WATCH THE PURSUIT STUMBLE BY WIRE: SUNSHINE NINE 4, ATHLETICS 3

Caminero, DeLuca, and Simpson strung three consecutive two-out doubles in the first — Simpson's two-hit night lifting his average to .310, level with Houston's Alvarez atop the American's race — and Nick Martinez made the early four stand for his fifteenth victory, the first Ray to the figure since Eflin in 2023. White and Bolte answered with solo thunder before Kelly, Booser, and Sulser (saving on the closer Baker's day of rest) shut the door. With the Yankee defeat arriving by wire an hour earlier, the East's lead swells to four and a half; the house celebration, the wires confide, now features a spinning wheel of forfeits, and last night's commanded DeLuca to hug the manager Cash mid-interview — "the first time he actually brought me in," the outfielder reported with satisfaction.

SCHERZER, TWO-AND-FORTY YEARS OLD, HOLDS THE LINE FOR FIVE — THE CANADIANS STOP DETROIT'S RUN AT SIX AND KEEP THEIR CANDLE LIT: CANADIANS 5, BENGALS 1

The Bengals' six-game surge, sung in yesterday's columns, died at Toronto against the oldest arm in the argument: Max Scherzer, carrying an earned-run figure north of six, gave five innings of one-run ball because his club had no other choice and every need. "Our backs are against the wall," said the future Hall man. "We've got to come out fighting and clawing." Straw's go-ahead single in the fourth and a sixth inning fattened by two Detroit errors did the scoring; Varland sealed his four-and-thirtieth. The ledger stays stern — a game and a half from the last chair, with the tiebreaker now Chicago's, not theirs, since the Central's flip re-sorted the quarry — and the Canadians open at Texas Friday with Cease and Soriano loaded in order.

EOVALDI OUT OF THE BULLPEN TO 'COME TOGETHER' — FOUR SPOTLESS INNINGS, THE LAST ELEVEN MEN RETIRED, AND THE WEST IS A DEAD HEAT: TEXAS NINE 7, HUB NINE 3

With Gore fighting spasms through four labored innings, the Arlington crowd rose in the sixth to a mid-game apparition: Nathan Eovaldi, the co-ace turned emergency fireman, whose four scoreless innings retired the final eleven Boston men and made him the first Texas pitcher to win while throwing four or more spotless frames to end a game since 2007. "It felt almost like a closer coming into the game," said the manager Schumaker. "But it was early — you're just not used to feeling it." Contreras' two-run homer, set up by a shrewd challenge of the machines, was most of Boston's evening; a three-run seventh off the faltering Hub bullpen was most of Texas'. The Texas nine draw dead level with Houston at .500 apiece atop the West — though the Silver Boot tiebreaker is Houston's, nine games to four — while Boston's wild-card cushion holds at five over Chicago.

RAVE AND MASSEY SUPPLY THE THUNDER AND HOUSTON GOES QUIETLY — NOUGHT-FOR-NINE WITH MEN IN SCORING POSITION, AND THE WEST'S THRONE IS SHARED: MISSOURIANS 5, ASTROS 2

John Rave's two-run homer in the fourth and Michael Massey's solo blow in the eighth headed a Kansas City evening that Houston met with a shrug — nought-for-nine with runners in scoring position, one man past second base through seven innings, and a seventh defeat in ten games. Peña's three hits were the local consolation; the veteran Walker, mired at nought-for-nineteen, spoke the clubhouse's creed ("We're in a spot to be in the postseason, and that's what we're fighting for") while the manager Espada compressed the strategy to two words: "Win tomorrow." The Astros share the West with Texas at six-and-seventy wins and losses apiece, tiebreaker in hand, with Atlanta arriving for the weekend.

THE CROWNED CREAM CITY NINE DECLINE THE HANGOVER — FOUR TWO-OUT SINGLES, YELICH'S TWO-STRIKE TURN, AND VICTORY NUMBER FIVE-AND-NINETY: CREAM CITY NINE 5, ALLEGHENYS 4

A day after the champagne, Milwaukee won in its own dogged dialect: four consecutive two-out singles from the order's cellar in the second, then a seventh-inning rally of walk, single, walk, and fielder's choice before Christian Yelich lined a two-strike single the opposite way for the lead. Lowe's two-run homer and Flores Jr.'s solo blow had put the Alleghenys briefly ahead; Uribe and Megill closed the door, the latter's eight-and-twentieth save. The larger designs — Henderson's capped start, the hundred-win arithmetic, Harrison's audition this very afternoon — stand in the October desk above.

CROW-ARMSTRONG STRIKES TWICE MORE AND PASSES SWEET-SWINGIN' BILLY OUTRIGHT — BREGMAN FALLS A SINGLE SHY OF THE CYCLE: CUBS 8, ATLANTAS 4

The chase this paper entered Tuesday at 'level with Billy Williams' lasted exactly one more home game: Pete Crow-Armstrong homered twice — his three-and-fortieth and four-and-fortieth — and tripled besides, passing Williams' 1970 figures outright for the most home runs (and, at one-and-eighty, the most extra-base hits) by a left-handed batter in all the Cubs' annals. It was his tenth career game of ten or more total bases — and his sixth of the summer, tying Cruz's 2019 figure for the most such games in any single season the books have recorded. Alex Bregman doubled, homered, and tripled behind him, then flied out in the seventh with the cycle on the line — "I tried to hit a single. It's stupid. I should've just kept trying to hit a homer," he grinned, before nodding at his teammate: "Pete's on cycle watch when he wakes up in the morning." The rookie Ritchie absorbed the schooling for Atlanta, whose October designs the desk above weighs. The forty-forty ledger stands at seven-and-thirty steals with ten games left; Wrigley waits on three more thefts.

SNELL THROWS NINETEEN PITCHES AND THE CORONATION IS POSTPONED — THE REDLEGS BEAT THE CHAMPIONS' BULLPEN AT ITS OWN LONG GAME: REDLEGS 6, ANGELENOS 2

Needing a victory or a San Diego defeat to seal a thirteenth West flag in fourteen years, the champions got neither: Snell's single inning opened the door — the ward above has his groin and his prognosis — and seven innings of patchwork relief could not hold the line, De La Cruz's two-run homer in the third and Myers' solo blow in the fifth leading a thirteen-hit Cincinnati evening. Stewart and Friedl singled home the insurance while Halvorsen took the loss; Bubic, activated from the sixty-day shelf that very day, threw the ninth. The Angelenos remain nine clear of the Padres with the finale this afternoon — Wrobleski starting, the bullpen game moved up a day by necessity.

TEN INNINGS AT ST. LOUIS AND THE BAY NINE OUTLAST THE SAVE-LEADER HIMSELF — GILBERT'S TENTH SETTLES A GAME THE REDBIRDS TIED TWICE: BAY NINE 6, REDBIRDS 5

Twice St. Louis clawed level — two in the seventh on an error and a wild pitch, two in the ninth on Fermín's sacrifice fly and Bernal's sharp single — and twice was made to pay for the impertinence, Drew Gilbert's two-run homer in the tenth off O'Brien, the National's co-leader in saves, deciding it. Cox stole two bases and singled two home in the seventh — one of them a gift of Walker's errant throw — Kuhnel sealed his eighth, and Saggese's sacrifice fly in the tenth bought the Redbirds back only the one. Two straight now for the Bay nine, playing out an orphaned September with evident professional pride.

NINE RUNS AT DENVER AND THE TEENAGER'S NAME IN THE HISTORY BOOKS — THE PADRES RETURN TUESDAY'S SCORE WITH INTEREST: PADRES 9, DENVER NINE 3

Two nights after the Denver nine snapped their eight-game streak by a 9-3 score, the Padres returned the identical figure with the ledger reversed: Salas' two historic blows — the milestone desk above has the full accounting — headed a thirteen-hit evening, France and Taylor driving two apiece and Harris legging a triple. Robbie Ray gave six innings of three for his thirteenth victory, throwing to the twenty-year-old for the first time and liking it fine. The third wild-card chair is San Diego's by three and a half over Arizona — four in the loss column, the figure that matters — with the season's final series at Petco still fated for the two of them.

MARSEE'S ELEVENTH AND A CAUGHT-STEALING FOR THE FINAL OUT — THE FLORIDIANS TAKE THE SERIES AND THE DESERT NINE TAKE THE CONSEQUENCES: FLORIDIANS 4, DESERT NINE 3

Jakob Marsee homered, doubled, stole a base, and drove in two, and Miami led from the second inning and never gave it back — though Arizona's three solo answers, Smith, Moreno, and Arenado in turn, kept the evening honest to its final pitch, when the catcher Mack threw out the pinch-runner Lawlar stealing to end it with the tying run erased. "We did our math, we did our work, and we felt like we were going to be able to steal that very, very easily," said the manager Lovullo, whose club went nought-for-six with men in scoring position, "and it didn't happen." The save was Alcantara's first, as the clubhouse desk sings above. The Desert nine fall three and a half behind San Diego with the Yankees arriving Friday; the frustration, by the starter Kelly's own account, sits "about the same place as you guys see it."

RALEIGH DRIVES IN THREE AND THE SERAPHS' BRIEF SURGE IS ENDED — SEATTLE PLAYS THE SPOILER'S PART WITH FEELING: MARINERS 7, SERAPHS 2

Cal Raleigh collected a sacrifice fly, a run-scoring double, and a run-scoring single — three driven in all — and Seattle broke a 2-2 evening open with three in the fifth and two in the sixth, two Anaheim errors assisting the arithmetic. Naylor stole two bases among his two hits; the reliever Vargas took the decision behind Kirby, and Kikuchi absorbed the loss. The Seraphs' two-game surge of earlier in the week, noted in these columns, is ended; the same clubs give way tonight to Minnesota's arrival.

The Thursday tables, then — re-drawn at the top of two divisions in a single evening. In the American: clinched Tampa Bay holds the East by four and a half over clinched New York, Boston ten and a half astern; the Central is Cleveland's by half a game over Chicago for the first time since Independence Day, with the tiebreaker still Chicago's, as the lead columns sing; and the West is a dead heat, Houston and Texas level at six-and-seventy wins apiece with the Silver Boot tiebreaker in Houston's keeping. The wild-card row is wholly re-sorted: New York and Boston seated in comfort, the last chair now Chicago's by one over Texas, with Toronto a game and a half back and Baltimore two and a half. In the National: Atlanta by four and a half over Philadelphia, its magic number five; crowned Milwaukee by ten and a half over Chicago; the champions by nine over San Diego, their coronation postponed a night, as the card records. The wild-card ledger: the Cubs at the row's head by a game and a half, Philadelphia half a game behind them, San Diego in the third chair by three and a half over Arizona — four in the loss column — with Miami seven and a half back and Pittsburgh eight. Tonight's bill is nine engagements, verified against the schedule, and the desk commends: at 12:35 the audition of Harrison at Pittsburgh, with October places open; at 1:10 Rasmussen and the Sunshine nine try for a sixteenth sweep against the Athletics; at 7:40 Detroit calls at Chicago, where the Pale Hose may retake a share of the Central without Cleveland lifting a finger, the new leaders being idle; and at 8:05 Gray, seventeen-and-five, carries Boston's salvage errand into Texas. Ten mornings remain to the season's final page on the seven-and-twentieth; the Wild Card rounds open on the nine-and-twentieth. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

~ THE HERALD ~
